position: both — *a good book*, *The book is good*; in the senses 'large in amount' and 'complete and thorough' only before a noun (*a good hour*, *a good look*)
comparison: irregular — *better*, *best*
takes: *at* + noun or *-ing* for skill (*good at chess*); *with* + people or things you handle (*good with kids*); *for* + the person or thing it helps (*good for your heart*); *to* + a person for kindness (*good to me*); *of* + person + *to*-infinitive (*good of you to come*); *about* after *feel* (*feel good about it*); *to*-infinitive (*good to know*); *that*-clause (*It's good that you called*)
contrast: *Good* is the adjective and *well* the adverb: *She's a good driver* / *She drives well* — *She drives good* is heard in casual speech but is marked wrong in careful English. After linking verbs use *good*: *It looks good*, *That smells good*. *I feel good* means happy or in good shape; *I feel well* means not sick. In American English *I'm good* means *I'm fine* and, when you are offered something, *No, thanks*. Skill is *good at* (not *good in*), kindness is *good to*, benefit is *good for*: *She's good at math*, *He was good to me*, *Fish is good for you*. The forms are *better* and *best*, never *gooder* or *more good*. Russian *добрый* about a person is usually *kind*, not *good*.

senses.gloss: Of high quality; done or made well.
examples: That was a really *good* movie.
The food here is *good*, but the service is slow.
Her second novel is even *better* than the first.

senses.gloss: Skillful; able to do something well.
examples: She's *good* at math.
He's a *good* driver — I always feel safe with him.
My dad is really *good* with his hands.

senses.gloss: Pleasant or enjoyable.
examples: Did you have a *good* time at the party?
I've got some *good* news.
The weather should be *better* this weekend.

senses.gloss: Morally right; kind and honest.
examples: He's a *good* man who would never lie to you.
It was *good* of you to drive me home.
She's always been *good* to her neighbors.

senses.gloss: Well-behaved — of a child or an animal.
examples: Be *good* for the babysitter, okay?
The kids were very *good* on the flight.
Who's a *good* dog?

senses.gloss: Beneficial; having a good effect on your health or well-being.
examples: Walking every day is *good* for you.
Too much soda isn't *good* for your teeth.
Getting out of the city was *good* for her.

senses.gloss: Suitable or convenient.
examples: Is this a *good* time to talk?
Tuesday is *good* for me.
What's the *best* way to get to the airport?

senses.gloss: Acceptable; good enough for what is needed.
examples: "Let's meet at seven." "Sounds *good*."
The photo isn't perfect, but it's *good* enough for the website.
Your English is *good* enough for the job.

senses.gloss: Attractive or pleasing to look at.
examples: You look *good* in that jacket.
The new kitchen looks really *good*.

senses.gloss: Valid; still able to be used.
examples: This ticket is *good* for one ride.
The coupon is *good* until the end of the month.

senses.gloss: Still fresh; not spoiled.
examples: Is this milk still *good*?
The bread should be *good* for another day or two.

senses.gloss: Strong or sensible enough to be accepted.
examples: Do you have a *good* reason for being late?
That's a *good* point.
She had a *good* excuse for missing the meeting.

senses.gloss: Fine; satisfied and not needing anything — informal American.
examples: "How are you?" "*Good*, thanks."
"Do you want more coffee?" "No, I'm *good*."
We're *good* — you don't owe me anything.

senses.gloss: Large in amount; at least as much as stated.
examples: The hotel is a *good* ten miles from the beach.
We spent a *good* deal of money on repairs.
It took a *good* hour to get there.

senses.gloss: Complete and thorough.
examples: Take a *good* look before you sign anything.
What I need is a *good* night's sleep.
She had a *good* cry and felt a lot better.

senses.gloss: Sure to pay back money owed — in *good for*.
examples: I'll lend you fifty bucks — I know you're *good* for it.
Don't worry, his brother is *good* for the money.

position: both — *a bad idea*, *The idea is bad*
comparison: irregular — *worse*, *worst*
takes: *at* + noun or *-ing* for skill (*bad at math*); *with* + things you handle (*bad with names*); *for* + the person or thing harmed (*bad for your back*); *about* after *feel* for guilt (*feel bad about it*); *for* after *feel* for pity (*feel bad for him*); *to*-infinitive (*It's bad to skip breakfast*); *that*-clause (*It's bad that nobody told her*)
contrast: *Bad* is the adjective and *badly* the adverb: *a bad singer* / *She sings badly*. After linking verbs use *bad*: *It smells bad*, *I feel bad*. *I feel bad about it* means guilty; *I feel bad for him* means sorry for him; *I feel badly* is common in American speech but disliked by careful writers. The forms are *worse* and *worst* — *more bad* is wrong, and *badder* is only slang. *Not bad* is praise: it means *pretty good*. Russian *мне плохо* is *I feel sick* or *I feel bad*, not *I'm bad*, which means *I behave badly*. *My bad* (my mistake) is a slang noun, not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Of low quality; not good.
examples: The service at that restaurant is really *bad*.
His handwriting is so *bad* I can't read it.
That was the *worst* movie I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Unpleasant or unwelcome.
examples: I'm afraid I have some *bad* news.
It's been a *bad* day.
The weather got *worse* in the afternoon.

senses.gloss: Serious or severe.
examples: She has a *bad* cold.
There was a *bad* accident on the interstate.
Traffic is *worst* on Friday afternoons.

senses.gloss: Harmful.
examples: Smoking is *bad* for you.
Is coffee *bad* for kids?
Sitting all day is *bad* for your back.

senses.gloss: Not suitable or convenient.
examples: Is this a *bad* time to talk?
Friday is *bad* for me — how about Monday?
He picked the *worst* possible moment to ask for a raise.

senses.gloss: Not skillful.
examples: I'm *bad* at math.
He's terrible with names, and I'm even *worse*.
She's a *bad* driver.

senses.gloss: Morally wrong; evil.
examples: He's not a *bad* person — he just made a mistake.
Lying to her was a *bad* thing to do.

senses.gloss: Naughty — of a child or an animal.
examples: *Bad* dog! Get off the couch!
Were the kids *bad* for the sitter?

senses.gloss: Rude or offensive — of words and language.
examples: Mom, he said a *bad* word!
The movie is rated R for *bad* language.

senses.gloss: Spoiled or rotten.
examples: The milk has gone *bad*.
Throw out any *bad* apples.

senses.gloss: Guilty or embarrassed about something you did — with *feel*.
examples: I feel *bad* about forgetting your birthday.
Don't feel *bad* — it wasn't your fault.

senses.gloss: Sorry about someone else's trouble — in *feel bad for*.
examples: I feel *bad* for her — she worked so hard for that job.
We all felt *bad* for the new guy.

senses.gloss: Unwell; or injured and painful.
examples: I've had a *bad* back for years.
He has a *bad* knee, so he can't run.
She was feeling *worse* by evening, so we called the doctor.

senses.gloss: Unfortunate; a pity — in *too bad*.
examples: It's too *bad* you can't come.
Too *bad* — the store's already closed.

senses.gloss: Not valid; not able to be paid or collected.
examples: He paid for the car with a *bad* check.
The bank lost millions on *bad* loans.

position: attributive only — *the far end*, *the far right*; in *It isn't far* and *How far is it?* the word is the adverb
comparison: irregular — *farther*, *farthest* for distance; *further*, *furthest* for distance or degree
contrast: As an adjective *far* stands before a noun and usually means the more distant of two sides or ends: *the far side of the lake*. It is not the everyday word for *далёкий* — say *a distant country* or *a faraway place*; *a far country* sounds literary. *It's not far* and *How far is it?* are adverb uses, and plain *It's far* is informal — *It's a long way* is safer. The comparison splits: *farther* and *farthest* are for physical distance; *further* and *furthest* work for distance too and are the only choice for *additional* (*further questions*). *The far right* is a political label (*крайне правые*), not a direction.

senses.gloss: Being the more distant of two sides, ends or edges.
examples: Our room was at the *far* end of the hall.
They live on the *far* side of town.
We took the *farthest* table from the kitchen because it was quieter.

senses.gloss: At the most distant part of a region.
examples: She grew up in the *far* north of the state, near the Canadian border.
The storm hit the *far* western part of the state.

senses.gloss: Holding the most extreme political views — in *far left* and *far right*.
examples: The party has moved toward the *far* right.
*Far*-left groups organized the protest.

senses.gloss: Distant in space or time — mostly literary, and in *the far future*.
examples: Robots may do that kind of work in the *far* future.
Pilgrims came from *far* lands to see the shrine.

senses.gloss: Very different from something — in *a far cry from*.
senses.ru: совсем не то, что; далеко не
examples: The new apartment is a *far* cry from our old place.
The final product was a *far* cry from what they promised.

position: both — before a noun in every sense (*a little house*); after a verb mainly for age (*when I was little*), since *small* sounds more natural there for size (*The house is small*)
comparison: irregular — *less*, *least* for amount; for size *smaller*, *smallest*, with *littler*, *littlest* in informal speech
contrast: *Little* often carries feeling (*a cute little house*, *a nasty little man*); *small* is neutral and is the word to compare: *a smaller room*, rarely *a littler room*. For amount, *little* with an uncountable noun is negative, like *мало*: *We have little time*; *a little* is positive, like *немного*: *We have a little time*. Many grammars call this amount use a determiner, and its forms are *less* and *least*. With countable nouns use *few*: *few friends*, not *little friends*. In *a little tired* the word is an adverb, and in *I speak a little* a pronoun.

senses.gloss: Small in size.
examples: They live in a *little* house by the lake.
Cut the potatoes into *little* pieces.
That's the *littlest* puppy I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Young.
examples: We have two *little* kids.
I lived in Ohio when I was *little*.

senses.gloss: Younger — of a brother or sister.
examples: This is my *little* brother, Sam.
Her *little* sister just started college.

senses.gloss: Short in time or distance.
examples: Can you wait a *little* while?
Let's take a *little* walk after dinner.

senses.gloss: Not important; minor.
examples: It's just a *little* problem — don't worry about it.
She always notices the *little* things.

senses.gloss: Not much; hardly any — before uncountable nouns.
examples: There's *little* hope of finding them now.
He showed *little* interest in the job.
We had *less* time than we expected.

senses.gloss: Used to show affection or annoyance.
examples: What a sweet *little* baby!
Get out of my room, you *little* brat!

position: both — *an old house*, *The house is old*; in the senses 'former' and 'known for a long time' only before a noun (*my old boss*, *an old friend*)
comparison: -er/-est — *older*, *oldest*; *elder*, *eldest* only for rank in a family
contrast: Age is *be* + number + *years old*, never *have*: *She is ten years old*, not *She has ten years*. Before a noun the phrase is hyphenated and singular: *a ten-year-old girl*. Position changes the meaning: *an old friend* is a friend you have known for years, not an elderly one, and *my old job* is my former job. *Older* and *oldest* are the normal forms, in families too (*my older brother*); *elder* and *eldest* go only before a noun and never take *than*. About people, *old* can sound blunt — *older* or *elderly* is politer.

senses.gloss: Having lived for a long time; not young.
examples: An *old* man was feeding the pigeons.
My grandparents are getting *old*.
She's the *oldest* person in our town.

senses.gloss: Of a particular age.
examples: How *old* are you?
Our son is six years *old*.
My sister is two years *older* than me.

senses.gloss: Having existed or been used for a long time; not new.
examples: I wear my *old* sneakers for yard work.
They bought an *old* farmhouse and fixed it up.
This is the *oldest* building in the city.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the distant past; traditional.
examples: It's an *old* family recipe.
The town has kept many of its *old* customs.

senses.gloss: Former; from an earlier time in your life.
examples: I ran into my *old* boss at the mall.
Do you miss your *old* school?
In the *old* days, nobody locked their doors.

senses.gloss: Known for a long time.
examples: Mike is an *old* friend from college.
The two teams are *old* rivals.

senses.gloss: Boring because it keeps happening — in *get old* and *the same old*.
examples: His jokes are getting *old*.
It's the same *old* story every Monday.

senses.gloss: Used informally to show affection or for emphasis.
examples: Good *old* Dave — he always shows up.
Just grab any *old* shirt.
He drives a big *old* pickup truck.

position: both — *a late train*, *The train is late*; in the sense 'dead' only before a noun (*her late husband*)
comparison: -er/-est — *later*, *latest*; *latter* and *last* are separate words
takes: *for* + an event (*late for work*); *to* + an event or place, common in American speech (*late to class*); *with* + something owed or due (*late with the rent*)
contrast: Position changes the meaning: *her late husband* is dead, but *Her husband is late* means he has not arrived yet. *Lately* is not the adverb of this word — it means *recently*: *I've been busy lately*; *He arrived late* uses the adverb *late*. Russian *уже поздно* is *It's late*, with the adjective. *Later* is the comparative (*a later flight*) and *latest* the superlative, which also means *newest*; *latter* (the second of two) and *last* (final) have their own entries.

senses.gloss: Arriving or happening after the expected or arranged time.
examples: Sorry I'm *late* — the traffic was terrible.
The bus was twenty minutes *late*.
Don't be *late* for your interview.

senses.gloss: Happening after the usual time.
examples: We had a *late* lunch.
Spring was *late* this year.
Is there a *later* flight to Denver?

senses.gloss: Near the end of a day or of a period of time.
examples: It's getting *late* — let's go home.
The house was built in the *late* 1800s.
She's in her *late* thirties.

senses.gloss: Dead, especially recently.
examples: The book is dedicated to her *late* husband.
The foundation was started by the *late* senator.

position: both — after a verb for distance and time (*The station is near*); before a noun only in set uses (*the near future*, *a near miss*) and in the comparative and superlative (*the nearest store*)
comparison: -er/-est — *nearer*, *nearest*
contrast: Do not put plain *near* before a noun to mean *close by*: say *a nearby store* or *a store nearby*, not *a near store* — though *the nearest store* is correct. *Near the park* is the preposition and *Come near* the adverb; neither is this adjective. American English says *near the beach*, rarely *near to the beach*. *A near miss* is an accident that almost happened. For family, *a close relative* is far more common in the US than *a near relative*.

senses.gloss: Only a short distance away.
examples: The hotel is quite *near* — we can walk.
Is the subway station very *near*?
Let's eat at the *nearest* diner.

senses.gloss: Soon in time.
examples: Prices will rise in the *near* future.
The holidays are *near*, and the stores are packed.

senses.gloss: Almost happening or almost complete.
examples: That was a *near* miss — the truck almost hit us.
The game ended in *near* silence.
The flood was a *near* disaster for the town.

senses.gloss: Being the closer of two sides.
examples: Park on the *near* side of the street.
We swam from the *near* bank to the island.

senses.gloss: Closely related — formal.
examples: Only *near* relatives can inherit under the will.
She has no *near* family left.

position: both — in the sense 'sick' mostly after a verb (*She's ill*) or with an adverb before a noun (*seriously ill patients*); in the senses 'bad' and 'hostile' only before a noun (*ill effects*, *ill will*)
comparison: irregular — *worse*, *worst*
contrast: In everyday American English *sick* is the usual word and *ill* is more formal: *I'm sick* / *She is seriously ill*. *An ill child* sounds stiff — say *a sick child* — but an adverb makes *ill* normal before a noun (*terminally ill patients*). In British English *sick* often means *vomiting*; in American English it means *ill*. Before a noun *ill* usually means *bad*, not *sick*: *ill effects*, *ill will*. The forms *worse* and *worst* belong to both *ill* and *bad*: *She got worse*. *Ill-* in compounds (*ill-advised*, *ill-treated*) is the adverb, and *the ills of society* is a noun.

senses.gloss: Sick; not in good health.
examples: Her father is seriously *ill*.
I felt *ill* after the long bus ride.
By Tuesday she was *worse*, so we took her to the ER.

senses.gloss: Bad or harmful.
examples: The drug has no known *ill* effects.
He retired early because of *ill* health.

senses.gloss: Unfriendly or hostile.
examples: I bear him no *ill* will.
There was a lot of *ill* feeling after the vote.

senses.gloss: Nervous and uncomfortable — in *ill at ease*.
examples: He looked *ill* at ease in a suit and tie.
Big parties make me feel *ill* at ease.

position: predicative only — *I'm not well*; before a noun only in medical phrases like *a well-baby visit*
comparison: irregular — *better*, *best*
contrast: The adjective *well* means *healthy*; the adverb *well* means *in a good way*: *I'm well* (not sick) / *She sings well*. *I feel well* is about health; *I feel good* is about health or mood, and in casual American English *I'm good* is the usual answer to *How are you?* The comparative is *better*: *I feel better*, not *more well*. Because it only follows a verb, *a well man* is wrong — say *a healthy man*. *Well* the noun (*колодец*) and the interjection (*Well, maybe*) are other words.

senses.gloss: Healthy; not sick.
examples: I'm not feeling *well* today.
Is your mother *well*?
She was sick last week, but she's *better* now.

senses.gloss: In a good or satisfactory state.
examples: All is *well* at home.
I hope all is *well* with you and your family.

senses.gloss: Lucky or a good thing, considering what happened — in *just as well*.
examples: It's just as *well* we left early — the roads got icy.
She didn't get the job, which was just as *well*, since she hated the commute.

senses.gloss: Sensible or advisable — formal.
examples: It would be *well* to get a second opinion.
It might be *well* to call ahead before you go.

position: both — *a better job*, *This one is better*
comparison: irregular — *better* is the comparative of *good* and *well*; the superlative is *best*
takes: *than* + noun or clause; *at* + noun or *-ing* (*better at math*); *with* + people or things you handle; *for* + the person or thing it helps; *to*-infinitive (*It's better to wait*)
contrast: *Better* is already comparative, so it never takes *more* or *very*: *much better*, *even better*, *a lot better*, not *more better* or *very better*. *I'm better* means *I have recovered*; *I'm good* only means *I'm fine*. *You'd better go* (*had better*) is a modal phrase, and *She sings better* is the adverb. *Better off* means *in a better situation, richer*: *We're better off without him*. Russian *лучший* is *better* when two things are compared (*a better car*) and *the best* for all others; careful English says *the better of the two*.

senses.gloss: Of higher quality, more pleasant or more suitable than someone or something else.
examples: This laptop is much *better* than my old one.
The weather is *better* today.
Would Friday be *better* for you?

senses.gloss: More skillful.
examples: She's *better* at chess than her brother.
He's *better* with kids than I am.

senses.gloss: Less sick; or fully recovered.
examples: Are you feeling *better* today?
My cold is *better*, but I still have a cough.
Stay home until you're completely *better*.

senses.gloss: More sensible or advisable.
examples: It's *better* to ask than to guess.
It would be *better* if you told her yourself.

senses.gloss: Most of something — in *the better part of*.
examples: I waited the *better* part of an hour.
They spent the *better* part of the day at the beach.

position: both — *the best pizza in town*, *Which one is best?*; before a noun it needs *the* or a possessive (*my best friend*)
comparison: irregular — *best* is the superlative of *good* and *well*; the comparative is *better*
takes: *at* + noun or *-ing* (*best at math*); *for* + the person or purpose it suits; *to*-infinitive (*It's best to wait*)
contrast: *Best* is already superlative: *the best*, *the very best*, never *most best*. Before a noun it needs *the* or a possessive — *She's the best student*, not *She's best student*. Without *the* it often means *most sensible*: *It's best to call first*. When only two things are compared, careful English uses *better*: *the better of the two*, though *the best of the two* is common in speech. *Do your best* and *at best* use the noun, and *She sings best* is the adverb.

senses.gloss: Of the highest quality; better than all others.
examples: This is the *best* pizza in town.
Emma has been my *best* friend since third grade.
It was the *best* day of my life.

senses.gloss: Most skillful.
examples: She's the *best* player on the team.
Who's *best* at math in your class?

senses.gloss: Most suitable or advisable.
examples: It's *best* to book early.
What's the *best* way to get downtown?
Do whatever you think is *best*.

position: both — *a worse problem*, *The problem is worse*
comparison: irregular — *worse* is the comparative of *bad* and *ill*; the superlative is *worst*
takes: *than* + noun or clause; *at* + noun or *-ing* (*worse at math*); *for* + the person or thing harmed
contrast: *Worse* is already comparative: *much worse*, *even worse*, never *more worse* or *badder*. Do not mix it up with *worst*: *This is worse than yesterday* (two things) / *This is the worst day ever* (all others). *Worse* ends in an s sound, *worst* in st. *Worse off* means in a worse situation, poorer. *She sings worse than I do* is the adverb.

senses.gloss: Of lower quality or less pleasant than someone or something else.
examples: The sequel is *worse* than the original.
The food was *worse* than I expected.
We couldn't have picked a *worse* day for a picnic.

senses.gloss: More serious or severe.
examples: The pain is *worse* at night.
Traffic is *worse* than usual today.
The problem is *worse* than we thought.

senses.gloss: Less skillful.
examples: I'm even *worse* at math than my brother.
He's *worse* with money than anyone I know.

senses.gloss: More sick; in poorer health.
examples: Grandpa got *worse* overnight.
If your fever gets *worse*, call the doctor.

position: both — *the worst day*, *Allergies are worst in spring*; before a noun it needs *the* or a possessive (*my worst fear*)
comparison: irregular — *worst* is the superlative of *bad* and *ill*; the comparative is *worse*
contrast: *Worst* compares something with all others; *worse* compares two: *the worst movie of the year* / *worse than the book*. Never *most worst*, and *baddest* is only slang. *The worst is over* and *at worst* use the noun. American English says both *if worse comes to worst* and *if worst comes to worst*.

senses.gloss: Of the lowest quality; worse than all others.
examples: That was the *worst* meal I've ever had.
He's the *worst* boss I've ever worked for.
It was the *worst* decision of her career.

senses.gloss: Most serious, severe or harmful.
examples: It was the *worst* storm in fifty years.
The *worst* part was waiting for the results.
Allergies are *worst* in the spring.

senses.gloss: Least suitable or convenient.
examples: This is the *worst* time to buy a house.
You picked the *worst* possible moment to call.

senses.gloss: Least skillful.
examples: I was the *worst* player on the team.
She's the *worst* at remembering birthdays.

position: both — *the farther shore*, *The lake was farther than we thought*
comparison: irregular — *farther* is the comparative of *far*; the superlative is *farthest*
contrast: In American English *farther* is for physical distance and *further* for distance or degree: *The school is farther than the library* (*further* is also fine here) / *further questions* (only *further*). Never use *farther* for *additional* — *farther information* is wrong. *We walked farther* is the adverb. Russian *дальнейший* is *further*, not *farther*.

senses.gloss: More distant.
examples: The beach was *farther* than it looked on the map.
Our new office is *farther* from home, so I leave earlier.

senses.gloss: Being the more distant of two sides or ends.
examples: They built a cabin on the *farther* shore of the lake.
The *farther* end of the field was flooded.

position: both — *the farthest point*, *Which planet is farthest from the sun?*
comparison: irregular — *farthest* is the superlative of *far*; the comparative is *farther*
contrast: *Farthest* is only for physical distance; *furthest* covers distance and also degree (*the furthest thing from my mind*). Before a noun it needs *the* or a possessive: *the farthest table*. *Who can throw the ball farthest?* is the adverb.

senses.gloss: Most distant.
examples: We sat at the *farthest* table from the stage.
Neptune is the *farthest* planet from the sun.
The *farthest* town on the route is about 200 miles away.

position: both — in the sense 'additional' only before a noun (*further details*); in the sense 'more distant' also after a verb (*The store is further than I thought*, *Nothing could be further from the truth*)
comparison: irregular — *further* is a comparative of *far*; the superlative is *furthest*
takes: *than* + noun or clause; *from* + a place or an idea, in the sense 'more distant'
contrast: *Further* in the sense *additional* has no *farther* twin: *further information*, *until further notice*, never *farther information*. For physical distance careful American writing prefers *farther*, but *further* is common and correct. *Let's discuss it further* is the adverb, and *to further your career* is the verb. Russian *дальнейший* and *дополнительный* are both *further*: *further steps*, *further questions*. *More further* is wrong.

senses.gloss: Additional; more.
examples: Call us if you have any *further* questions.
The office is closed until *further* notice.
Police are waiting for *further* information.

senses.gloss: More distant, in space or in degree.
examples: The hospital is *further* than the fire station.
The campsite was *further* from the lake than the website said.
Nothing could be *further* from the truth.

position: both — *the furthest house*, *Which town is furthest?*
comparison: irregular — *furthest* is a superlative of *far*; the comparative is *further*
contrast: For physical distance *furthest* and *farthest* both work, with *farthest* preferred in careful American writing. Only *furthest* is used for degree: *the furthest thing from my mind*. Before a noun it needs *the* or a possessive. *He went furthest in the tournament* is the adverb.

senses.gloss: Most distant.
examples: They live in the *furthest* house on the road.
Which of the moons is *furthest* from Jupiter?

senses.gloss: Least likely or least true — in *the furthest thing from*.
examples: Retirement is the *furthest* thing from my mind.
What he told the reporters was the *furthest* thing from the truth.

position: attributive only — *my elder sister*; after a verb only in *the elder of the two*, never *She is elder than me*
comparison: irregular — *elder* is a comparative of *old* used for rank in a family; the superlative is *eldest*
contrast: *Elder* goes only before a noun and never takes *than*: *my elder brother*, but *My brother is older than me*, not *elder than me*. American English uses *older brother* far more often; *elder* sounds formal. It is only for people, mostly in a family: *an older car*, not *an elder car*. *An elder* (a respected old person, a church leader) and *respect your elders* are noun uses. *Elderly* means *old*, not *older*.

senses.gloss: Older — of one of two members of a family.
examples: Her *elder* sister lives in Seattle.
He's the *elder* of the two brothers.
My *elder* son is in college now.

senses.gloss: Used to tell apart two well-known people with the same name, usually a father and son.
examples: The *elder* Bush was president from 1989 to 1993.
The *elder* Dumas wrote The Three Musketeers.

senses.gloss: Senior and respected because of age and experience — mainly in *elder statesman*.
examples: At eighty, he is the party's *elder* statesman.
She has become an *elder* stateswoman of the tech industry.

position: attributive only — *my eldest daughter*; also *the eldest* standing alone (*She's the eldest of four*)
comparison: irregular — *eldest* is a superlative of *old* used for rank in a family; the comparative is *elder*
contrast: *Eldest* is only for people, almost always in a family: *my eldest son*, but *the oldest building*, never *the eldest building*. *Oldest* works everywhere and is more common in American English. With only two children, *elder* is traditional (*the elder of the two*), though *eldest* is common in speech.

senses.gloss: Oldest — of three or more members of a family.
examples: Their *eldest* daughter just got married.
I'm the *eldest* of five kids.
As the *eldest* son, he took over the family farm.

position: attributive only — after *the*, *this* or a possessive (*the latter option*); *the latter* also stands alone for the second of two
comparison: not gradable — once a comparative of *late*, now fixed in meaning
contrast: *Latter* (rhymes with *matter*) and *later* (rhymes with *waiter*) are different words: *the latter half* is the second half; *a later date* is a date further in the future. Use *the former* and *the latter* only for two things; for three or more say *the last*. It is formal and mostly written — in speech Americans usually say *the second one*. *The latter* often stands alone: *Of the two plans, the latter is cheaper*.

senses.gloss: Being the second of two people or things already mentioned.
examples: In the *latter* case, you'll need to apply for a new passport.
Customers can pay online or by phone, and most choose the *latter* option.

senses.gloss: Nearer the end of a period of time.
examples: Sales picked up in the *latter* half of the year.
He spent his *latter* years in Florida.
The project is in its *latter* stages.

position: both — mostly before a noun (*the last page*); after a verb in *be last* (*She was last in line*)
comparison: not gradable — once a superlative of *late*; *the very last* adds emphasis
contrast: *Last week*, *last year* and *last Friday* take no article and mean the one before this one: *I saw her last week*. *The last week* means the past seven days, or the final week of something: *The last week has been crazy* / *the last week of June*. *Last* means *final* or *the one before now*, while *latest* means *newest*: *his last book* may be his final one, *his latest book* is his newest, with more to come. For news and updates say *the latest*, not *the last*. *At last* is an adverb phrase, *He finished last* uses the adverb, and *to last* is the verb.

senses.gloss: Coming after all others; final.
examples: Don't skip the *last* chapter.
She was the *last* person to leave the office.
The *last* train leaves at midnight.

senses.gloss: Just before this one — with *week*, *month*, *year*, *night* and days of the week, without *the*.
examples: We went to Boston *last* weekend.
*Last* night's game went into overtime.
I saw him *last* Tuesday.

senses.gloss: Most recent.
examples: The *last* time I saw her, she was still in high school.
Prices have doubled over the *last* few years.
His *last* email was pretty rude.

senses.gloss: Only remaining.
examples: Can I have the *last* cookie?
I spent my *last* ten dollars on gas.

senses.gloss: Least likely or least wanted.
senses.ru: последний (о ком или чём меньше всего ожидаешь)
examples: He's the *last* person I expected to see here.
A flat tire is the *last* thing I need right now.

position: attributive only — after *the* or a possessive (*the latest news*); *the latest* standing alone (*Have you heard the latest?*) is a noun use
comparison: -er/-est — *latest* is the superlative of *late*; the comparative is *later*
contrast: *Latest* means *newest, most recent*, and more may follow: *her latest album*. *Last* means *final*, or the one before now: *her last album* may be her final one. For news, trends and versions English says *latest*, not *last*: *the latest news*, *the latest update*. *At the latest* means *no later than*: *by Friday at the latest*. *Late* in the sense *dead* has no *latest*.

senses.gloss: Newest; most recent.
examples: Have you seen her *latest* movie?
Download the *latest* version of the app.
The *latest* polls show a close race.

senses.gloss: Happening after all others in time.
examples: What's the *latest* time we can check out?
The *latest* flight to Miami leaves at 10:40.
Friday is the *latest* date we can accept your application.

position: both — mostly before a noun (*the next day*); after a verb in *be next* (*You're next*)
comparison: not gradable — once the superlative of *nigh*, an old word for *near*
contrast: *Next week*, *next year* and *next Monday* take no article and mean the one after this one: *See you next week*. With *the*, *next* counts from some other time: *We arrived on Monday and left the next day*. *Next Friday* can be unclear in American speech — some people mean the coming Friday, others the Friday after — so *this Friday* is safer for the coming one. *Next* is about order and *nearest* about distance: *the next gas station* is the next one on your route, *the nearest gas station* the closest in any direction. *Next to* (*рядом с*) is a preposition, and *What happened next?* is the adverb.

senses.gloss: Coming right after this one in time or order.
examples: We'll cover that in the *next* chapter.
The *next* day, it snowed.
Who's *next* in line?

senses.gloss: Just after this one — with *week*, *month*, *year* and days of the week, without *the*.
examples: My parents are visiting *next* month.
*Next* summer we're going to Maine.
I have a dentist appointment *next* Thursday.

senses.gloss: Nearest in place; right beside.
examples: The music from the *next* room kept me awake.
She lives in the *next* town over.
The couple at the *next* table were arguing.

position: both — *the nearest hospital*, *Which exit is nearest?*
comparison: -er/-est — *nearest* is the superlative of *near*; the comparative is *nearer*
takes: *to* + noun (*the seat nearest to the door*)
contrast: *Nearest* is about distance, *next* about order: *the nearest exit* is the closest one, *the next exit* is the one you reach after this one on the highway. Unlike plain *near*, *nearest* stands freely before a noun: *the nearest store*, never *a near store*. In everyday American speech *closest* is more common. *To the nearest dollar* means rounded (*с точностью до доллара*).

senses.gloss: Closest in distance.
examples: Where's the *nearest* gas station?
The *nearest* hospital is forty miles away.
Take the seat *nearest* to the door.

senses.gloss: Closest in relationship or likeness.
examples: This is the *nearest* thing to real Mexican food in town.
His *nearest* relative is a cousin in Ohio.

senses.gloss: Rounded to a given unit — in *to the nearest*.
examples: Round the answer to the *nearest* whole number.
Prices are rounded to the *nearest* dollar.
